sources.entry: jax - A library for high-performance numerical computing with autodiff and JIT compilation.

summary.one_liner: JAX is a Python library for accelerator-oriented array computation and composable program transformations (autodiff, JIT compilation via XLA, and vectorization) aimed at high-performance numerical computing and large-scale machine learning.
summary.what_it_does: JAX differentiates native Python and NumPy functions, including through loops, branches, recursion, and closures, and supports reverse-mode (jax.grad) and forward-mode differentiation composable to any order. The jax.jit transform uses XLA to compile pure functions end-to-end for TPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators. The jax.vmap transform auto-vectorizes functions over array axes, which can be composed with grad and jit to get per-example gradients or Jacobians. The README also describes scaling across many devices through automatic parallelization, explicit sharding with jax.sharding types, and manual per-device programming with explicit collectives. The README describes JAX as a research project rather than an official Google product.
use_cases: automatic differentiation of numerical Python code
compiling NumPy-style programs for GPUs and TPUs
batching a function over array axes without manual loops
sharding machine learning training across many devices
notable: Composable transformations: grad, jit, and vmap can be nested arbitrarily
Differentiates through Python control flow such as if-statements and loops
Three scaling modes: automatic, explicit sharding, and manual per-device with collectives
Installable with hardware-specific extras for CPU, NVIDIA, AMD, TPU, and Intel GPUs
caveats: The README states it is a research project, not an official Google product, and warns to expect sharp edges
jax.jit constrains which Python control flow can be used inside compiled functions
GPU and platform support varies: Windows native has no NVIDIA or AMD GPU support, and several GPU paths are marked experimental
